sources.citation: Blench, Roger & Timothy Terna. 2026 [Wikipedia cites as 2025]. Aspects of the grammar of Zhire [zhi], a Plateau language of Central Nigeria. Circulation draft, printout February 9, 2026, 35 pp. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation (KWEF). https://www.academia.edu/164507054/
sources.note: Nothing on stress (0 hits for 'stress' in the 35-page text). §2 Phonology (pp. 3-4) covers consonants, vowels and tone only: 'Zhire has three levels of surface phonetic tone. However, it does not seem possible to find a neat minimal triplet to support this. Hence Kempton (2025) considers there are just two underlying tone levels, high and low.' Tone marks H, M, L and four contours are used; noun plurals are largely marked by tonal change.

sources.citation: Decker, Ken, Julius Dabet, John Muniru, Benard Abraham & Innocent Jonah. 2021. A Sociolinguistic Profile of the Zhire [zhi] Language of Kaduna State, Nigeria. Journal of Language Survey Reports 2021-008, 59 pp. Dallas: SIL International. https://www.sil.org/resources/archives/88036
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. §6.2 Phonetic inventories (pp. 10-11): 'there was no in-depth analysis of tones or other phonological features'; 'We have identified five tones: high [á], low [à], rising [ǎ], falling [â], and an unmarked mid tone. While tone has been marked in the transcription, it has not been included in the comparisons.' Three village varieties compared: Gindu, Fei, Hogyeng.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2010. The Shang language of Central Nigeria and its affinities [annotated wordlist]. Draft circulated for comment, printout August 31, 2010. Cambridge: KWEF. http://www.rogerblench.info/Language/Niger-Congo/BC/Plateau/Hyamic/Shang/Shang%20wordlist.pdf
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sister/closest variety (Shang, treated by Blench as relexified Zhire), not Zhire itself. §3.3 Tones (p. 2): 'Shang appears to have three level tones, plus a falling tone.' No mention of stress.

sources.citation: Yaro, Mary James. 2008 [Glottolog: 2010]. A contrastive analysis of tense formation and usage in Jaba and English language. MA thesis, Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, 83 pp. https://kubanni.abu.edu.ng/items/f8330ea9-9ad3-4c59-b63f-047258c39856
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Stress is discussed only for English (CONtract vs conTRACT as an example of phonological ill-formedness); for Kanyi it says only that tense is marked by tone: 'the Kanyi speaker uses tone to differentiate between the two tense forms. The rising tone is used to indicate a past tense and the falling tone is used to indicate a present activity'. No statement about Zhire/Kanyi word stress.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2006. 'You couldn't make it up': The phonology of Hyam. Draft circulated for comment, printout January 2, 2006, 13 pp. Cambridge: Mallam Dendo. https://www.rogerblench.info/Language/Niger-Congo/BC/Plateau/Hyamic/Hyam/Hyam%20phonology.pdf

sources.note: Sister language (Hyam), not Zhire; Zhire is mentioned only in the classification list (p. 1). No statement on stress for any Hyamic language.
